doc.title: Lonnie Liston Smith interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 9, 2021

title: Rahsaan Roland Kirk and the first recordings
summary: Smith recalls Rahsaan's multiple horns and clarinet week, and his first recordings with him at Van Gelder's studio.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Who were the great clarinetists? Favorites and rivals

blocks.x: You know I saw Rahsaan in probably 1968 or 9, and what a force of nature he was.

That’s a good way of putting it. Because Rahsaan, he had the nose flute, then he played the three horns, and you know it made sense because he’d make the harmony and everything. And oh I know one time we was on the road and he went to New Orleans, you know, like on vacation, him and his wife. And man when he came back, for a whole week all he wanted to do was play the clarinet. Because you know that’s the big thing in New Orleans. So you know that was interesting. So we used to say uh oh — for a whole week he played the clarinet. But you know Rahsaan, I think he was the first to play the three horns.
I believe you’re right. You know some fellas have done two but, yeah I kept thinking how the heck does he do that. And then I got to see him and I still didn’t believe it.

Oh yeah, I know. The way he hooked them up, then he had that nose flute. That was something. But it — because actually my first recordings we did “Here Comes the Whistleman” and “Please Don’t Cry Beautiful Edith.” And we did “Beautiful Edith” over
in VanGelder’s studio, which is fantastic. So those were my first two recordings with Rahsaan.
